findings.title: Denial cache blocks fallback for 30s after permission grants or folder-permission grants
findings.body: The new permDenialCache is keyed by (namespace, userUID, action, name, parent) with a 30s TTL and is consulted BEFORE the permCache check and the new DB-fallback path. Trace for the regression scenario: (T=0) user denied -> permDenialCache.Set(("dash1", "fold1")) and permCache holds empty data; (T=10) admin grants permission on dash1, or grants permission on fold1 which gives inherited access via checkInheritedPermissions; (T=15) user retries -> permDenialCache.Get HITS and returns Allowed=false, so neither permCache nor getIdentityPermissions is consulted. The very same PR adds a fallback that would otherwise have allowed this request immediately. Result: a user who was previously denied (directly OR via folder inheritance that has since been granted) stays denied for up to 30s, despite the freshly persisted grant. This is the same window the fallback was designed to eliminate, so the new denial cache directly negates the PR's own improvement for the permission-grant case. The PR should either (a) invert the check order so permCache/fallback runs first, (b) invalidate the denial entries on role/permission changes, or (c) at minimum document this trade-off.

findings.title: Server-side fix only applies in-proc; remote mode still hides newly created dashboards behind 30s client cache
findings.body: The PR removes the authlib client cache for the in-proc case by passing NoopCache (lines 101-105) so every request reaches the server-side Check (which now has the cache-fix logic). But the remote branch at lines 160-167 still wires authzlib.WithCacheClientOption with cache.NewLocalCache{Expiry: 30s}. Because the client caches the whole CheckResponse, the bug the PR is fixing ("dash/folder creator can't access the dashboard/folder that they've just created") is NOT fixed for remote deployments: a creator's first Check on their new dashboard will be served from the 30s client cache, not from the server. Either the in-proc change should be applied symmetrically to remote, or the 30s TTL should be reduced to ~0 with explicit invalidation when permissions change.

findings.title: No test covers the "user is granted access to a previously denied resource" scenario
findings.body: TestService_CacheCheck exercises: cache-hit allow, cache-miss DB fallback, outdated-cache DB fallback, and explicit denial-cache hit. None of these exercise the precise regression introduced by permDenialCache: deny a user at T=0 (sets denial cache), then grant the permission (or grant the parent folder), then issue another Check and assert it is allowed. Adding such a test would currently FAIL against the new code, surfacing the regression described in the first finding. Without it, the trade-off between denial cache and the DB-fallback fix is not pinned down and could silently regress in future.

findings.title: Test stores map[string]bool{"...": false} but comment claims it "Allow[s] access"
findings.body: In the subtest "Should deny on explicit cache deny entry", the comment "Allow access to the dashboard to prove this is not checked" sits above s.permCache.Set(..., map[string]bool{"dashboards:uid:dash1": false}). The value false is falsy, so in checkPermission the truthiness check scopeMap[t.scope(req.Name)] returns false and the lookup behaves identically to the key being absent. The comment is therefore wrong: the entry is not an "allow" entry. If the intent of the test is to show that the denial cache overrides an allow decision from permCache, the cached value should be true (e.g., map[string]bool{"dashboards:uid:dash1": true}) so the contrast with the denial cache is unambiguous.
